1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5.background: It is named after the Austrian master Ernst Falkbeer, who played it in an 1851 game against Adolf Anderssen.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit Accepted
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5.strategy: The principal answer: White takes the pawn and leaves Black to show that a lead in development and an exposed White king are worth it. White's task is to catch up in development, even handing the extra pawn back at the right moment, while Black plays for activity.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.Nf3.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Blackburne Attack
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.Nf3.background: The second most common move for White against the Falkbeer Countergambit, after 3.exd5, and considered sound.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops first and covers h4, so there is no queen check on that square, and keeps the central tension instead of winning a pawn at once. If Black takes on e4, the knight takes the pawn on e5 and the material is level again. A sound way to meet the countergambit.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.Nc3.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Milner-Barry Variation
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.Nc3.strategy: Protects e4 with a developing move instead of settling the centre, but Black takes the pawn anyway. After the knight recaptures, the loose f4 pawn is a target and White's kingside is weakened, so Black has the easier game.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.d4.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Hinrichsen Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once but leaves both the e4 and f4 pawns unprotected: Black simply takes a pawn with ...exf4 or ...dxe4, and White has nothing to show for the sacrifice.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 exf4.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Modern Transfer
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 exf4.strategy: Takes the f-pawn, so the material is level again: the pawn on f4 cramps White's kingside, and Black's pieces aim at the pawn on d5. White keeps the central pawns, and Black has to make activity count in a position with a loosened white king.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 c6.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Nimzowitsch-Marshall Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 c6.background: Frank Marshall introduced 3...c6 to master play, beating Richard Teichmann at Ostend in 1905, but it is usually attributed to Aron Nimzowitsch, who played it successfully against Rudolf Spielmann at Munich in 1906. It languished in obscurity for many years; John Nunn is its most notable advocate, and it is now the most commonly played move after 3.exd5.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 c6.strategy: Challenges the d5 pawn at once, trading material for piece activity. If White hands the pawn back and consolidates, White keeps the better pawn structure and the better endgame prospects, so Black must make the activity count in the middlegame against the weakened kingside.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Staunton Line
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4.background: The line was once considered good for Black and scored well.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4.strategy: The traditional idea: the pawn takes the f3 square from White's king's knight and Black plays for a lead in development against the exposed king. But the pawn is also a target, and White's way of attacking it gives White the better game, so the line is played less than it once was.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 Bc5.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Miles Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop towards f2 instead of recapturing on d5, so Black has simply given a pawn for activity. With no direct threat yet, White can keep the pawn, though taking a second one on e5 invites a queen check on h4.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 c6 4.dxc6.strategy: Grabs a second pawn instead of developing. That wins material but leaves White's king uncastled with a loosened kingside, and Black's lead in development grows with every move; the greedy capture is dubious, and developing a piece is the better way to meet the pawn offer.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 c6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and declines the second pawn: the knight covers e4 and defends the d5 pawn, so White keeps what it has taken and makes Black prove the compensation. After ...exf4 the pawns are level and the game is roughly even.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 c6 4.Qe2.strategy: Attacks the e5 pawn a second time from the open e-file, but the queen stands in front of the uncastled king and becomes a target for Black's developing moves. The game ends up level, with White's extra pawn balanced by Black's lead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 c6 4.dxc6 Bc5.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Pickler Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 c6 4.dxc6 Bc5.strategy: The point of the gambit: instead of recapturing on c6, Black develops the bishop on a diagonal that eyes f2 and g1, so White cannot castle short. Black is two pawns down, but White's kingside is loose and Black's pieces come out faster.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 c6 4.dxc6 Nxc6.strategy: The solid recapture: the knight develops and guards e5 against the f4 pawn, and the queen's checks on the kingside stay available. Black is still a pawn down, but White's king is in the centre and the kingside is loosened, so Black plays for quick development rather than quick material.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 c6 4.dxc6 bxc6.strategy: Recaptures with a pawn and leaves the knight at home, so the move spends a tempo on material rather than on a piece. It also leaves isolated pawns on a7 and c6. Black is still a pawn down and has fewer pieces out to attack the loosened kingside.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.d3.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Charousek Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.d3.background: Against 3...e4 it gives White some advantage, which is why that line fell out of favour.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.d3.strategy: The reply that took the shine off Black's gambit: it challenges the cramping pawn on e4 at once and frees the queen's bishop. White keeps the extra pawn on d5 and, once the e4 pawn is gone, develops freely; Black has to prove the activity is enough.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops, guards the d5 pawn and attacks e4 in one move, without committing the d-pawn. The cost is that the c1-bishop stays shut in for now, and Black gets time to defend the e4 pawn with a developing move.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.Bb5+.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Anderssen Attack
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.Bb5+.strategy: Checks at once to make Black spend a move on the king, but the bishop stands exposed on b5 and the check wins nothing lasting: Black can answer with a pawn move that hits both the bishop and d5, while the e4 pawn still cramps White's development.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.d3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a purpose: the knight guards the e4 pawn and attacks the pawn on d5 at once, so Black keeps the gambit going. Black commits to the advanced pawn on e4, which White will now try to dissolve, and relies on a lead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.d3 Qxd5.strategy: Takes the pawn back at once and keeps e4 defended with the queen, so material is level and the bind stays. The queen is out early and White gains time on it with Nc3, but ...Bb4 answers with a pin. A fair alternative that trades some of the gambit's initiative for material.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.d3 exd3.strategy: Gives up the advanced pawn for White's d-pawn and with it the bind that makes the gambit work. After Qxd3 the d5 pawn is protected again, so Black stays a pawn down with the cramping pawn gone, and has only a lead in development to play for.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.d3 Nf6 5.dxe.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Charousek Gambit Accepted
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.d3 Nf6 5.dxe.strategy: Takes the pawn: White keeps the extra material and removes the cramping pawn, at the price of opening the position. Black's knight retakes with an active piece, and the game becomes a race between Black's development and White's extra pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.d3 Nf6 5.Nd2.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Charousek Gambit, Keres Variation
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.d3 Nf6 5.Nd2.strategy: Develops and adds a second attacker to e4 without giving up the d3 pawn, but it leaves d5 with no defender, so Black can retake it at once. The knight also blocks the c1-bishop, so White's development gets no easier.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.d3 Nf6 5.Qe2.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Charousek Gambit, Old Line
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.d3 Nf6 5.Qe2.strategy: Adds the queen to the attack on e4, but the queen stands on the e-file in front of the uncastled king, where Black can gain time against it with the bishop or a check, and d5 is left without a defender.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.d3 Nf6 5.dxe.strategy: Regains one pawn and centralises the knight in one move, so White's extra pawn is the one on d5. No pawn can drive the knight from e4, and Black's pieces are ready to come out with threats against the king that stands in the middle.
Checks before recapturing, but White answers Bd2 and after the bishops trade, Nxd2 leaves a knight guarding e4. Black cannot win the pawn back at once and White is two pawns up.
Loses the queen for two pawns: the pawn on e4 attacks d5, so exd5 wins it, and ...Nxd5 only takes that pawn back.

Brings the knight to its natural square now that the e4 pawn no longer controls it. It covers h4 against queen checks and keeps the extra pawn, and White hopes to finish development before Black's pieces become dangerous.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.d3 Nf6 5.dxe.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Charousek Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.d3 Nf6 5.dxe.strategy: Pins the knight on e4 against the king and attacks it, but the pin is harmless: Black defends the knight and wins back the d5 pawn in one move. The queen then stands in front of the uncastled king, and White has used a tempo without solving the development problems.
Develops but leaves h4 uncovered: ...Qh4+ forces g3, and ...Nxg3 forks the rook on h1 and the bishop on f1 and wins material. Moving the king instead leaves it exposed in the middle of the board.

Black's compensation for the pawn: the bishop eyes f2 and g1, so White cannot castle short and the king stays in the centre while Black's pieces keep coming. Black needs this initiative, since the pawn deficit is real.

Develops the bishop and defends the knight on e4, so a pin on the e-file cannot win it. The bishop does not aim at f2 or stop White castling, so the main line's pressure is gone and White keeps the extra pawn.

Puts the queen behind the knight on the e-file, so any knight move gives a discovered check and a careless Nc3 loses the queen. It neither wins the d5 pawn back nor stops White castling, so Black is still a pawn down with the queen out early.

Recaptures on d5, which levels the material, and guards the pinned knight from the centre in the same move. The knight cannot move while the pin lasts, so a developing move that attacks the queen is what Black has to watch for.

Defends the pinned knight with a developing move, which takes the sting out of the pin on the e-file. It leaves the d5 pawn with White, so Black stays a pawn down, and the bishop on f5 can be chased by a pawn push.

Guards the knight with the queen and stands behind it on the e-file, so the pin on the king becomes a pin on the queen and a knight move only offers a queen trade. Black does not regain the d5 pawn and stays a pawn down.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops, guards the e4 pawn and attacks the pawn on d5 in one move. Black keeps the gambit going with the advanced pawn, and White's extra pawn is now a target that has to be defended or given back.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.Nc3 Bf5.strategy: Defends the e4 pawn with a developing move, so Nxe4 would lose the knight to the bishop's recapture. Black keeps the bind, but the queen eyes the d5 pawn, which the knight defends, so the extra pawn is safe for now.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.Nc3 Qe7.strategy: Defends the e4 pawn with the queen and uses the open e-file: a pawn push to d3 is met by ...exd3 with check. The queen comes out early, no minor piece develops and the d5 pawn is not challenged, so White keeps the extra pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.d3.strategy: Attacks the e4 pawn a second time while the knight already guards d5, so Black's pawn is attacked twice and defended once. It reaches the main line's plan by another move order: White removes the cramping pawn and keeps the extra material.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.Qe.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Rubinstein Variation
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.Qe.background: One of the common alternatives to the main line 4.d3 in the old Falkbeer line 3...e4.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.Qe.strategy: Brings a second attacker, the queen, to the e4 pawn, with the knight on c3 as the first. The queen stands on the e-file in front of the uncastled king, where the c8-bishop can gain time against it, and Black must act at once to keep the e4 pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.Bb.strategy: Checks and develops the bishop, but it spends a tempo on a piece that Black can challenge with ...c6, which also attacks the d5 pawn. White keeps the extra pawn without doing anything about the e4 pawn that cramps White's development.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.d3.strategy: Develops with a pin: the knight on c3 cannot move without exposing the king, and that knight both guards d5 and attacks e4. White has to deal with the pin before anything else.

Takes the pawn back at once, but the knight was the only defender of e4, so Nxe4 takes a pawn in return. Black is still a pawn down and the cramping pawn is gone, so the move gives up the gambit's point for active pieces.

Takes the d3 pawn to dissolve the tension, but White recaptures and the e4 clamp is gone. Black stays a pawn down, having traded the advanced pawn for White's d-pawn, with only ...Bb4 left to play for.

Breaks the pin by putting the bishop on d2, a developing move that keeps the knight on c3 guarding d5 and attacking e4. The bishop on d2 is now exposed to a pawn push from Black, so White has to be ready for a sharp reply.

Takes the cramping pawn and builds a pawn chain on e4 and d5, but the knight on c3 is pinned and cannot recapture, so ...Nxe4 regains a pawn at once. White stays a pawn up, with the king still in the centre and Black's pieces active.

Supports the pinned knight with a second piece instead of unpinning it, and keeps the bishop and queen free. The pin on c3 stays, though, and the king is still in the centre, so Black can keep adding pressure to the knight.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.d3.name: King's Gambit Declined: Falkbeer Countergambit, Charousek Gambit, Morphy Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.d3.strategy: Attacks the bishop and f2 with the pawn, giving a second pawn to drag the bishop off d2 and revive the pin on the knight on c3. For two pawns Black gets open lines and a lead in development against the kingside.

Trades the bishop for the knight that guards d5 and attacks e4, which eases the pressure on the e4 pawn. White recaptures with the bishop, which gains a long diagonal aimed at f6 and g7, so Black has given up its active bishop for little.

Takes the d3 pawn to open the position, but Bxd3 recaptures with a developing move and Black stays a pawn down with the e4 clamp gone. Bd2 has broken the pin, so the bishop on b4 has little left to work with.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn the knight guards and wins it for the moment. If the knight recaptures, the loose f4 pawn gives Black a target, and White's weakened kingside gives Black the easier game.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Defends the d5 pawn and develops, adding a second attacker on e4 while keeping the tension in the centre instead of releasing it. White has to decide how to resolve it, and Black gets a comfortable, balanced open game.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.Nc3 d4.strategy: Pushes the pawn at the knight, gaining space and keeping material level once the knight moves and the f4 pawn falls. The d4 pawn cramps White, but the tension in the centre is gone and the pawn has to be defended.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4.name: Dunst Opening: Grünfeld Defence, Steiner Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4.strategy: Regains the pawn at once, but the f4 pawn is still loose: Black takes it with ...exf4 and is a pawn up. White has no lead in development to make up for it, and the king is still exposed.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.fxe5.strategy: Takes back at once, trading the f-pawn for Black's e-pawn, so material is level and the f-file opens. Other moves fall a pawn behind. The e4 pawn is attacked by the knight, so Black has to defend it.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d3.strategy: Offers a second pawn for development, but Black simply takes the f4 pawn: dxe4 Qxd1+ Kxd1 leaves Black a pawn up with White's king stuck in the middle.
